object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: An event tracked by the incident process, arising from an alert and/or customer ticket, that goes through states triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique, never reused? ... Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an incident, prefixed INC- followed by a sequence.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: A signal from the monitoring platform (or a manually raised record) indicating a potential incident.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.
If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for an alert, sourced from the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A support ticket raised in the support system, which may relate to an incident.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: Unique identifier for a support ticket.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Severity
object_types.definition: Technical impact / blast radius classification of an incident, from SEV1 (everyone down) to SEV4 (cosmetic, one region).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: Priority
object_types.definition: Customer urgency classification of an incident, from P1 to P4, based on who is affected and SLA/contractual impact.

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The lifecycle state of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.

object_types.name: Person
object_types.definition: A named individual who can act as incident commander for the duration of an incident.

source_references.excerpt: The incident commander. One person, named, and it's a role for the duration, not a job title.

object_types.name: Team
object_types.definition: A team that owns a service on a standing basis.

source_references.excerpt: A team. Services are owned by teams. People move.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system/service in the catalogue that can be affected by incidents and is owned by exactly one team.

ambiguities.description: Severity and Priority are described as changing over time ('Severity gets revised', history kept 'in the timeline, as events'), but the model captures only current severity/priority on the Incident. Should a full history of severity/priority changes be modeled as a separate fact type/entity (e.g., SeverityChange events) rather than just current-state attributes?

source_references.excerpt: Can either change during the incident? ... Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. ... In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The 'monitoring' state that Owen mentions sitting between mitigated and resolved was explicitly rejected as an official state ('It's not in the dropdown'), but is informally used by people. Should this be flagged as a potential future/unofficial state, or documented as pure social convention with no modeling impact? Confirm the five-state enumeration is complete and stable.

source_references.excerpt: There's also "monitoring," which sits between mitigated and resolved. ... If it's not in the system I'm not modelling it. Five states.

ambiguities.description: Classification of incidents caused by customer misconfiguration (vs genuine reliability events) is explicitly parked as an undecided business rule -- no classification concept exists in the current model, but stakeholders anticipate one will be needed. This is a known gap pending a decision by Ravi.

source_references.excerpt: Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: The duplicate-of ring constraint acyclic/no-chain rule is stated as the intended rule but explicitly 'not enforced' in practice, and two-deep chains have been observed. Should the model enforce acyclicity strictly (rejecting the current reality), or model it as a soft/aspirational constraint separate from the hard irreflexive and single-primary constraints?

source_references.excerpt: It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Alert creation from a manual observation ('an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record') suggests Alert may have a subtype distinction (automated monitoring alert vs manual alert), which is not modeled -- both share the same AlertId reference scheme. Is a separate 'origin type' attribute on Alert needed?

source_references.excerpt: If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.

ambiguities.description: Ticket-to-Incident link cardinality is not fully specified: 'support gets three tickets in the same two minutes' suggests multiple tickets can relate to one incident, but whether one ticket can also relate to multiple incidents (e.g., if later merged) is unclear. Similarly for Alert-to-Incident cardinality.

source_references.excerpt: Or both, which is the common one -- the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.
